If your devices are close to the router, connect them to the 5 GHz network. You’ll often see an immediate, dramatic speed increase. Streaming devices, gaming consoles, and laptops in the same room as the router should almost always be on 5 GHz.

If your router uses “band steering” (one network name for both bands), it may be putting your devices on the wrong band. Check your router settings to see if you can split them into separate names.

Update Your Router’s Firmware

Router manufacturers regularly release firmware updates that fix bugs, improve performance, and patch security holes. Many people never update their router, running firmware that’s years out of date.

Log into your router’s admin panel (usually by typing something like 192.168.1.1 into your browser), find the firmware or update section, and check for updates. Some routers do this automatically — make sure that setting is turned on.

Change Your WiFi Channel

In apartment buildings and dense neighborhoods, everyone’s WiFi is fighting for the same channels. It’s like a crowded highway with too many cars.

For the 2.4 GHz band, only channels 1, 6, and 11 don’t overlap with each other. If your neighbors are all on channel 6, switching to 1 or 11 can help.

You can scan nearby networks using a free app like WiFi Analyzer (Android) or the built-in tools on most computers. Look for the least crowded channel and switch to it in your router settings.

On 5 GHz, this is less of an issue since there are far more channels available.

Reduce Interference and Clutter

Every device in your home that emits radio waves is potentially interfering with your WiFi. That includes:

  • Bluetooth speakers and headphones
  • Wireless security cameras
  • Smart home devices
  • Older cordless phones

You don’t need to get rid of these, but keep them away from your router. A few feet of distance can make a real difference.

Consider a Mesh System or Extender

If your home is large, has thick walls, or has multiple floors, a single router may simply not be enough. This is where mesh WiFi systems shine.

A mesh system uses multiple units placed around your home that work together to create one seamless network. Unlike old-school extenders, mesh systems don’t require you to manually switch networks as you move around.

They’re not cheap — expect to spend $150 to $400 for a good system — but for larger homes, they’re often the single most effective upgrade you can make.

If your budget is tight, a traditional WiFi extender can help, but placement is critical. Put it roughly halfway between your router and the dead zone, not in the dead zone itself.

Check What’s Eating Your Bandwidth

Sometimes your WiFi isn’t slow — it’s just being used up. Common bandwidth hogs include:

  • 4K video streaming (uses up to 25 Mbps per stream)
  • Cloud backups running in the background
  • Large game downloads
  • Someone else’s video calls

Log into your router and look at connected devices. You might find a neighbor using your network (change that password), or a forgotten device downloading updates.

When to Call Your Provider

If you’ve tried everything above and your wired speed is also slow, the problem is likely on your provider’s end. Call them with your speed test results ready. Be specific: “I’m paying for 300 Mbps and getting 40 Mbps on a wired connection.”

That’s a much more effective conversation than “my internet is slow.”

A Quick Checklist

Before you spend money on new gear, run through this list:

  1. Move your router to a central, open, elevated spot
  2. Connect nearby devices to the 5 GHz band
  3. Update your router’s firmware
  4. Change your WiFi channel
  5. Move interfering devices away from the router
  6. Check for bandwidth hogs on your network
  7. Test again

Most people find that steps 1 through 3 solve the majority of their problems. If they don’t, you’ll at least know exactly what’s wrong — and that makes it much easier to fix.

item.title: How to Soundproof a Room on a Budget: 12 Cheap Fixes
item.description: Block noise without wrecking your wallet. Learn how to soundproof a room on a budget using towels, weatherstripping, rugs, and smart DIY tricks that work.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

You don’t need to spend $3,000 on professional acoustic panels to stop hearing your neighbor’s dog at 6 a.m. Most of the noise leaking into your room comes through a handful of predictable weak points — gaps around doors, thin windows, and bare floors — and you can fix the worst of them for less than the cost of a nice dinner.

Here’s the thing most soundproofing guides won’t tell you: you’re not trying to block all sound. You’re trying to reduce it enough that it stops bothering you. That shift in mindset is what makes a budget approach actually work. A 50% reduction in perceived noise is often the difference between “I can’t sleep” and “I barely notice it.”

I’ve helped friends soundproof apartments, home offices, and a bedroom above a drum-practicing teenager. The tricks below are the ones that actually moved the needle without a contractor or a credit card limit increase.

First, Understand What You’re Fighting

Sound travels two ways, and they need different solutions.

Airborne noise is what you hear from TVs, conversations, and music. It moves through the air and slips through gaps, cracks, and thin materials. This is the easiest and cheapest type to block.

Impact noise is footsteps, dropped objects, and vibrating bass. It travels through the physical structure of the building. This is harder to stop, but you can still reduce it.

Before buying anything, walk around your room and find the leaks. Stand in the corner, listen, and ask: where is the sound coming from? Nine times out of ten, it’s one of these:

  • The gap under your door
  • Single-pane windows
  • Unsealed electrical outlets
  • Bare hardwood or tile floors
  • Thin interior walls

Fix the cheapest leaks first. You’ll often get 70% of the benefit for 10% of the cost.

Cheap Fixes Under $30

Seal the Gaps Around Your Door

This is the single highest-impact, lowest-cost fix. A standard door has a half-inch gap at the bottom and often thin gaps around the frame. Sound pours through all of them.

  • Door sweep or draft stopper: A $10 adhesive sweep or a rolled towel at the base cuts a surprising amount of noise. A double-sided draft stopper (the kind that slides under the door) works even better.
  • Weatherstripping: Foam or rubber weatherstripping tape around the door frame costs about $8 and takes ten minutes to install. It seals the sides and top.
  • Door snake: The old-fashioned fabric tube filled with rice or sand still works. It’s ugly, but it’s $5.

Total cost: under $25. Expected result: a noticeable drop in hallway and adjacent-room noise.

Weatherstrip Your Windows

If you have single-pane windows, you’re basically living with a hole in your wall. You can’t replace them on a budget, but you can:

  • Apply removable caulk or rope caulk around the frame edges each winter. It peels off cleanly in spring.
  • Use window insulation film (the shrink-wrap kind) on the inside. It costs about $15 for a kit and creates an air gap that dampens sound.
  • Hang heavy curtains. A thick, lined curtain absorbs sound and blocks some of it from entering. Thrift-store curtains layered over cheap blackout panels work well.

Block Your Electrical Outlets

This one surprises people. Outlets and light switches are holes in your wall, and sound travels right through them. Remove the cover plate, and you’ll often find a gap between the electrical box and the drywall.

  • Acoustic putty pads cost about $2 each and are designed exactly for this. You mold them around the back of the outlet box.
  • Childproof outlet plugs add a tiny bit of mass and cost almost nothing.
  • Foam gaskets made for outlet covers are $5 for a pack of ten.

Do every outlet on the noisy wall. It’s a 20-minute job with a screwdriver.

Cheap Fixes Under $100

Add Mass to Your Walls

Sound hates mass. The heavier and denser a surface, the harder it is for sound to pass through. You can add mass cheaply with:

  • Moving blankets: Harbor Freight and similar stores sell them for $8–$15 each. Hang them on the wall with grommets or a curtain rod. They won’t look like a design magazine, but they work.
  • Bookshelves: A wall lined with full bookshelves is a surprisingly effective sound barrier. If you already own books, this is free. Leave a small air gap between the shelf back and the wall.
  • Old rugs: Hang a heavy rug on the wall. Thrift stores sell them for $10–$20.

Treat the Floor

If you’re dealing with noise from below or you want to stop sound from bouncing around your own room:

  • Area rug with a thick pad: This is the best bang-for-buck floor treatment. A rug alone helps; a rug plus a felt or rubber pad helps a lot more.
  • Interlocking foam mats: The kind sold for home gyms cost about $25 for 24 square feet. They’re great for kids’ rooms and home offices.
  • Carpet remnants: Check local carpet stores for remnants. You can often get a large piece for $30–$50 and have it bound or just lay it down.

Upgrade Your Door

If your door is hollow-core (knock on it — if it sounds empty, it is), it’s doing almost nothing. Options:

  • Add a layer of mass-loaded vinyl (MLV) to the door’s surface. A 4x8 sheet runs about $40–$60. It’s heavy and awkward, but effective.
  • Hang a soundproof blanket over the door on a rod. These cost $30–$50 and are designed for this purpose.
  • Replace the door with a solid-core one if you can find a used one at a Habitat ReStore. Used solid doors go for $20–$40.

Free and Nearly Free Tricks

  • Rearrange your furniture. Put your bed, desk, or couch against the shared wall. A heavy piece of furniture absorbs and blocks sound.
  • Close interior doors. Obvious, but people forget. Every closed door is another barrier.
  • Turn on a fan or white noise machine. Masking noise is often more effective than blocking it. A box fan costs nothing to run and covers a lot of frequencies. Free white noise apps work too.
  • Talk to your neighbor. Sometimes the noise is a fixable habit — a TV against a shared wall, a washing machine on a spin cycle at midnight. A polite conversation costs nothing.

What NOT to Waste Money On

  • Egg cartons. They do almost nothing for soundproofing. They’re a myth. Save your money.
  • Cheap foam panels. The thin, colorful acoustic foam tiles you see online are for reducing echo inside a room, not for blocking noise from outside. They won’t stop your neighbor’s bass.
  • “Soundproof paint.” It’s marketing. Paint doesn’t have the mass to block sound.

A Realistic Budget Plan

If you have $50, do this in order:

  1. Seal the door gaps ($20)
  2. Add outlet gaskets ($5)
  3. Put a rug down ($25)

If you have $150, add:

  1. Window film and heavy curtains ($40)
  2. Moving blankets on the shared wall ($30)
  3. A white noise machine ($30)

If you have $300, add:

  1. A used solid-core door ($40)
  2. MLV on the door ($50)
  3. A second layer of curtains or blankets ($50)

Each step builds on the last. You don’t have to do everything at once.

The Bottom Line

Soundproofing on a budget is really about sealing, adding mass, and masking. Seal the gaps first — they’re the cheapest and most effective fix. Add mass where you can with rugs, blankets, and bookshelves. Then mask whatever’s left with white noise.

You won’t achieve studio silence for $100. But you can absolutely go from “unlivable” to “totally fine,” and that’s usually all anyone actually needs. Start with the door. You’ll be surprised how much difference a $10 draft stopper makes.

item.title: Home Cybersecurity Tips: Protect Your Family in 2024
item.description: Practical home cybersecurity tips to protect your family, Wi-Fi, and smart devices. Learn password, router, and phishing defenses that actually work.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

In 2016, a Mirai botnet built from hacked home routers and IP cameras knocked major websites like Twitter and Netflix offline for hours. The devices weren’t targeted because their owners were important — they were targeted because they were easy. Default passwords, outdated firmware, and forgotten settings turned ordinary living rooms into weapons.

That’s the uncomfortable truth about home cybersecurity: you don’t have to be a target to become a victim. Most attacks are automated and indiscriminate. They scan the internet for weak points, and a home network with a factory-default router password is about as weak as it gets.

The good news? You don’t need a security team or an IT degree. You need a Saturday afternoon, a bit of patience, and the willingness to change a few habits. Here’s what actually matters.

Start With Your Router — It’s the Front Door

Your router is the gateway to every device in your home. If someone controls it, they control everything behind it. Yet most people set it up once and never touch it again.

Change the Default Credentials Immediately

Every router ships with an admin username and password, and those defaults are public knowledge. Lists of them circulate freely online. If you’re still logging in with “admin/admin,” fix that today. Log into your router’s admin panel (usually at 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1), find the settings, and set a unique password — ideally a passphrase you don’t use anywhere else.

Update the Firmware

Router manufacturers release firmware updates that patch security holes. Many routers don’t update automatically. Check your router’s admin panel for a firmware update option, or visit the manufacturer’s website. If your router is more than five or six years old and no longer receives updates, consider replacing it. An unsupported router is a permanent open door.

Turn Off WPS and Remote Management

Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) was designed for convenience, but its PIN-based method is vulnerable to brute-force attacks. Disable it. Similarly, turn off remote management unless you specifically need it — it exposes your router’s admin page to the entire internet.

Build Better Password Habits

Weak and reused passwords are behind a huge share of account takeovers. When one site gets breached, attackers take those email-and-password combos and try them everywhere else. This is called credential stuffing, and it works because so many people reuse passwords.

Use a Password Manager

A password manager generates and stores long, random passwords for every account. You only need to remember one strong master password. Popular options include Bitwarden (free and open-source), 1Password, and Dashlane. This single change eliminates the reuse problem entirely.

Turn On Two-Factor Authentication

Two-factor authentication (2FA) means a stolen password alone isn’t enough to break in. You’ll also need a code from your phone or a hardware key. Enable it on your email first — your email is the master key to your digital life, since password resets for everything else flow through it. Then add it to banking, social media, and cloud storage.

Prefer an authenticator app or hardware key over SMS codes when possible. SMS can be intercepted through SIM-swapping attacks, though it’s still far better than nothing.

Stop Using Security Questions With Real Answers

“Mother’s maiden name” and “first pet” are often findable on social media. When a site forces security questions, treat them like passwords: use random strings stored in your password manager.

Recognize Phishing Before It Hooks You

Phishing remains the most common way attackers get in. The modern versions are polished — correct logos, convincing language, and urgent deadlines.

The Telltale Signs

  • Urgency: “Your account will be closed in 24 hours.”
  • Mismatched links: Hover over a link (without clicking) and check the actual domain. “amazon-support.net” is not Amazon.
  • Unexpected attachments: Invoices you didn’t request, shipping notices for packages you didn’t order.
  • Generic greetings: “Dear Customer” instead of your name.

The Golden Rule

Never click a link in an unexpected message. Instead, open a new tab, go directly to the company’s website, and check your account there. If something’s genuinely wrong, you’ll see it. This one habit defeats most phishing attempts.

Secure Your Smart Home Devices

Smart TVs, doorbells, thermostats, and baby monitors are computers — often poorly secured ones. The 2016 Mirai attack proved how dangerous a house full of unpatched gadgets can be.

  • Change default passwords on every smart device, no exceptions.
  • Update firmware when prompted, and check for updates on devices that don’t notify you.
  • Put devices on a guest network. Most routers let you run a separate guest Wi-Fi network. Connect smart devices there so if one gets compromised, it can’t reach your laptops and phones.
  • Disable features you don’t use. Remote access, microphones, and cameras you never check are liabilities, not conveniences.

Keep Everything Updated

Software updates are boring, which is exactly why attackers love it when people skip them. Updates patch known vulnerabilities — holes that criminals already know how to exploit.

Turn on automatic updates for your operating system, browser, and phone. For everything else, set a monthly reminder to check. That includes your router, smart devices, and any apps you use regularly.

Back Up Your Data — The 3-2-1 Rule

Ransomware doesn’t just hit businesses. Home users get hit too, often through a malicious download or a compromised remote desktop. The defense is simple: have backups.

Follow the 3-2-1 rule — three copies of important data, on two different types of media, with one copy stored offsite or in the cloud. An external drive plus a cloud backup covers most families. Test your restore process occasionally; a backup you can’t restore isn’t a backup.

A Quick Household Checklist

  • Router admin password changed from default
  • Router firmware updated
  • WPS and remote management disabled
  • Password manager in use across the family
  • 2FA enabled on email, banking, and social accounts
  • Smart devices on a separate guest network
  • Automatic updates on for all major devices
  • Backups running and tested

Work through it one line at a time. None of these steps require technical expertise, and each one closes a door attackers rely on.

The Bottom Line

Home cybersecurity isn’t about being paranoid — it’s about being inconvenient to attack. Criminals scan for easy targets, and every step you take pushes you further down their list. Change the defaults, update your gear, use better passwords, and think before you click. Do those four things consistently, and you’ll be safer than the vast majority of households online.

Start with your router tonight. It takes fifteen minutes, and it’s the highest-value move you can make.

item.title: Best Home Printers: 7 Picks That Won't Waste Your Money
item.description: Shopping for a home printer? Compare the best inkjet, laser, and tank models for documents, photos, and tight budgets—plus ink costs to watch.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The last printer I bought came with a “starter” ink cartridge that died after 40 pages. Forty. The replacement set cost almost as much as the printer itself. That’s the dirty secret of the printer aisle: the cheap box on the shelf is rarely the cheap machine to own.

So before you buy, flip the math. A $79 inkjet with $65 cartridges is a worse deal than a $200 tank printer that runs for pennies a page. This guide breaks down the best home printers by what you actually print—school essays, tax forms, birthday photos, or all three—and flags the ink costs that manufacturers bury in the fine print.

First, Answer Three Questions

Skip this and you’ll overpay. Every good printer recommendation starts here.

1. What do you print most? Text documents and shipping labels point to laser. Photos and color-heavy school projects point to inkjet. A true mix needs a tank inkjet or a color laser.

2. How often do you print? If it’s once a month, inkjet printheads can clog between jobs. Laser toner sits for months without drying out. Occasional printers should lean laser or a tank model with self-cleaning cycles.

3. What’s your real cost per page? Do the math before buying:

  • Standard inkjet cartridge: $30–$45 for 200–300 pages = roughly 12–18 cents per page
  • Tank inkjet: $13–$20 per bottle, yielding 3,000–7,500 pages = under 1 cent per page
  • Laser toner: $60–$90 for 1,200–3,000 pages = 3–7 cents per page

That gap adds up. Print 20 pages a week and a tank printer can save you $100+ per year over a cartridge inkjet.

Best Overall for Families: Tank Inkjet

For most households juggling homework, recipes, and the occasional photo, a refillable tank inkjet is the sweet spot. Models like the Epson EcoTank and Canon MegaTank lines ship with two to three years of ink in the box. No chip-locked cartridges, no panic runs to the office supply store before a project is due.

Watch for: Print speed. Tank printers are slower than cartridge models, often 10–15 pages per minute in black. If you’re printing a 30-page packet, make coffee. Also check whether the model has a flatbed scanner—the cheapest tanks are print-only.

Best for: Families printing 50+ pages a month who want color without the cartridge tax.

Best for Documents Only: Monochrome Laser

If 90% of your printing is text—forms, tickets, contracts, school essays—a black-and-white laser is the most reliable machine you can buy. They don’t clog. They spit out 30+ pages per minute. And third-party toner is cheap and plentiful.

A budget monochrome laser from Brother or HP typically runs $100–$150, and a high-yield toner cartridge can push 3,000 pages. That’s years of printing for most homes.

The catch: No color. If your kid needs a poster with colored headings, you’re out of luck. Some families solve this by pairing a cheap laser with a budget color inkjet for the rare color job.

Best for: Remote workers, students, and anyone who prints mostly black text.

Best for Photos: Dedicated Photo Inkjet

Photo printers are a different animal. The good ones use six or more ink colors, including light cyan and light magenta, which smooth out skin tones and gradients that standard four-color printers turn grainy.

Expect to pay $200–$500, and expect ink to be expensive—photo printing always is. The trade-off is prints that actually look like photographs instead of faded office copies. If you only print a few 4x6 snapshots a month, consider a print service instead; the math rarely favors owning a photo printer for low volume.

Best for: Scrapbookers, hobbyist photographers, and anyone framing their own prints.

Best Budget Pick: Compact Inkjet Under $100

Sometimes you just need a printer, cheap, today. A basic inkjet from Canon or HP will handle color documents and casual photos for under $100. Just go in with clear eyes: the included cartridges are half-empty, replacements are pricey, and you may spend more on ink in year one than on the printer.

Money-saving tip: Look for a model that accepts XL or high-yield cartridges. They cost more upfront but cut your cost per page by 30–50%. Also check whether your local library charges 10–15 cents per page—for very low volume, it’s genuinely cheaper to print there.

Features Worth Paying For (and Ones to Skip)

Worth it:

  • Auto-duplex printing — prints both sides automatically, halving your paper use
  • Wi-Fi and mobile printing — AirPrint and Mopria let you print from your phone without a computer
  • A real flatbed scanner — the feed-style scanners on cheap all-in-ones mangle receipts and book pages

Skip it:

  • Fax capability — you haven’t faxed anything since 2009
  • Touchscreen displays — a $40 upcharge for a feature you’ll use twice
  • “Instant Ink”-style subscriptions — convenient, but you’re locked into the manufacturer’s pricing and page caps

Three Mistakes That Cost You Money

Buying ink at the big-box store. Retail cartridges carry a huge markup. Ordering direct or from a reputable online seller often saves 20–30%.

Ignoring third-party ink (sometimes). For laser toner, reputable third-party brands are usually fine and cost half as much. For inkjet, results vary—clogging and printhead damage are real risks, so read recent reviews for your specific model.

Leaving the printer off for months. Inkjet printheads dry out and clog. Run a test page every two to three weeks, or use the printer’s built-in maintenance cycle. A clogged head can cost more to fix than the printer is worth.

The Bottom Line

Match the printer to your actual habits, not the shelf display. Print mostly text? Buy a monochrome laser and stop thinking about it. Print a mix for a busy household? A tank inkjet pays for itself within a year. Print photos seriously? Budget for a six-color photo printer and accept that ink is the cost of the hobby.

Whatever you choose, calculate the cost per page before you swipe your card. The cheapest printer is almost never the cheapest to own.

item.title: Best Mesh WiFi Systems for 2025: Real-World Picks
item.description: Shopping for the best mesh WiFi system? We break down top picks for every budget and home size, plus setup tips that actually fix dead zones.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

My brother-in-law spent $400 on a “gaming router” with six antennas, mounted it proudly in his basement office, and then called me two weeks later because his wife couldn’t hold a video call in the kitchen directly above him. That’s the fundamental problem with traditional routers: more antennas don’t beat physics. WiFi signal degrades as it passes through floors, walls, and appliances, and a single broadcast point—no matter how powerful—can’t cover a whole house evenly.

Mesh systems solve this by placing multiple small nodes around your home that talk to each other and hand your devices off seamlessly as you move. Instead of one loud voice shouting from the basement, you get a relay team. The catch is that “mesh” has become a marketing sticker slapped on everything from $60 toys to $1,200 three-packs, and they are not remotely equal. Here’s how to pick the right one without overpaying.

What Actually Matters in a Mesh System

Before brand names, understand the four specs that determine whether a mesh system will work in your house.

WiFi Standard: WiFi 6 vs. WiFi 7

WiFi 6 (802.11ax) is now the baseline and handles most homes beautifully. WiFi 7 (802.11be) is faster on paper, but you only benefit if your devices support it—and most phones and laptops from before 2024 don’t. If you’re buying for a household with a mix of older gear, WiFi 6 is the value play. If you’re wiring a new home office with current-gen laptops and want this purchase to last six-plus years, WiFi 7 is worth the premium.

The Backhaul Question: Wireless vs. Wired

This is the single most misunderstood term in home networking. The “backhaul” is the connection between your mesh nodes. If they talk wirelessly, your speed drops at each hop. If you can run Ethernet between nodes—even just between two of them—performance jumps dramatically and stays stable. Many people buy a mesh system, place nodes wirelessly in far corners, and wonder why speeds sag. If your house has coax outlets in multiple rooms, look into MoCA adapters; they turn existing cable wiring into a fast wired backbone.

Band Support: Tri-Band Beats Dual-Band for Wireless Setups

Dual-band systems share one 5GHz channel for both your devices and the node-to-node chatter. Tri-band systems dedicate an entire band to backhaul, which keeps your devices running at full speed. If you’re going fully wireless, tri-band is close to mandatory for anything above 2,500 square feet.

Ethernet Ports Per Node

Count them before you buy. A node with only one port means you can’t hardwire a desktop or game console at that location. Two or more ports per node is the sweet spot.

The Best Mesh WiFi Systems, by Situation

Best Overall for Most Homes: TP-Link Deco XE75

The XE75 hits the trifecta: tri-band WiFi 6E, a dedicated 6GHz backhaul, and three Ethernet ports per node. In real-world testing, it holds 500–800 Mbps at the far node in a 3,000-square-foot home with wireless backhaul—numbers that crush most dual-band rivals. It’s not the fastest system on this list, but it’s the one I recommend most often because it’s forgiving. Place the nodes imperfectly, and it still performs.

Best for Gigabit-and-Beyond Speeds: Amazon Eero Max 7

If you have a 2.5G or 5G fiber plan and want to actually use it, the Eero Max 7 is the cleanest path. Two 10-gigabit ports per unit, WiFi 7, and genuinely simple app management. The trade-off: it’s expensive, and Eero leans on subscription features (like advanced security) that other brands include free. Buy it if you value “it just works” over tinkering.

Best Budget Pick: TP-Link Deco X20 or X55

Under $150 for a three-pack, the X20 covers up to about 5,500 square feet in ideal conditions (realistically, expect solid coverage in a 2,000–2,500 square foot home). It’s dual-band WiFi 6, so wireless backhaul costs you some speed—but for streaming, browsing, and video calls, it’s plenty. The X55 adds a bit more headroom for households with 30+ connected devices.

Best for Apple Households: Linksys Velop or Netgear Orbi

Apple’s own AirPort line is long dead, but Linksys and Netgear both offer strong HomeKit integration, and Orbi’s tri-band systems remain favorites among people who want maximum throughput with minimal fiddling. Orbi’s dedicated backhaul has been its signature feature for years, and it still delivers.

Best for Renters and Small Apartments: Google Nest WiFi Pro

One or two nodes, WiFi 6E, and the simplest setup of any system I’ve used—literally plug in, scan a code, done. It’s overkill for a studio, but ideal for a 1,200-square-foot apartment with a dead zone in the bedroom.

Placement: Where Most People Get It Wrong

You can buy the best system on this list and still have bad WiFi if you place nodes badly. Three rules that fix 90% of problems:

  1. Don’t put nodes in the dead zone. Counterintuitive but true: a node needs a strong signal from the main router to relay a strong signal onward. Place it halfway between the router and the dead zone, not in the dead zone itself.
  2. Get nodes off the floor and out of cabinets. WiFi hates metal, concrete, and fish tanks. A node on a bookshelf beats one behind the TV every time.
  3. Space nodes 25–40 feet apart. Closer isn’t better—overlapping too tightly causes interference and roaming confusion.

A Quick Word on Wired Backhaul

If you’re renovating or building, run Cat6 Ethernet to two or three ceiling or wall locations now. A $200 mesh system with wired backhaul will outperform a $700 system running wirelessly, every single time. It’s the highest-ROI networking decision you can make, and it costs a fraction of what people spend chasing bigger antennas.

The Bottom Line

For most homes, the TP-Link Deco XE75 is the best mesh WiFi system you can buy right now—tri-band, WiFi 6E, wired-backhaul-friendly, and reasonably priced. Step up to Eero Max 7 if you have multi-gig internet and want zero fuss. Step down to the Deco X20 if your needs are simple and your budget is tight. Whichever you choose, spend fifteen minutes thinking about placement before you spend an hour in the app tweaking settings. The physics of your house matter more than the logo on the box.

item.title: Smart Doorbell Installation Guide: DIY in 90 Minutes
item.description: Learn how to install a smart doorbell yourself in about 90 minutes. Covers wiring, transformers, chime setup, Wi-Fi tips, and renter-friendly options.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

My neighbor spent $180 on a video doorbell, then paid an electrician another $150 to install it. The electrician was done in 40 minutes. That’s $225 an hour for a job that mostly involves a screwdriver, a phone, and knowing which breaker to flip.

Most smart doorbells are genuinely DIY-friendly — but only if you know the three things that trip people up: your existing transformer’s voltage, whether you have a mechanical or digital chime, and where your Wi-Fi actually reaches. Miss any of those and you’ll spend a Saturday afternoon troubleshooting instead of watching your porch from the couch.

This guide walks through the whole process in the order you’ll actually do it, with the checks that save you return trips to the hardware store.

Before You Buy: Three Checks That Save You a Headache

1. Test your existing transformer

Wired doorbells run on low-voltage power, usually stepped down from your home’s 120V supply by a transformer — often mounted near your electrical panel, in a closet, or attached to a junction box in the basement or garage.

Most modern video doorbells need 16–24V AC and at least 10–30VA (volt-amperes). Older homes frequently have 10V or 16V/10VA transformers, which cause symptoms like random reboots, night-vision flickering, or the doorbell simply refusing to power on.

How to check: Find the transformer (look for a small metal or plastic box with two low-voltage wires), then read the label. If it says 16V/10VA, plan on upgrading. A compatible 16V/30VA transformer costs about $20–25 and takes 15 minutes to swap if you’re comfortable with basic electrical work.

2. Identify your chime type

Pop the cover off your indoor chime. You’ll see one of two things:

  • Mechanical chime: Two metal bars and a solenoid plunger. These work with almost every smart doorbell, though some models need a “power kit” installed inside the chime to prevent buzzing or ghost rings.
  • Digital chime: A small speaker and circuit board. These are pickier. Check your doorbell’s compatibility list before buying — some brands support digital chimes natively, others require a bypass.

3. Check Wi-Fi at the door

This is the most overlooked step. Doorbells live outside, often on the far side of an exterior wall, and 2.4 GHz signal drops fast through brick, stucco, and metal siding.

Stand at your door with your phone and run a speed test. You want at least 2 Mbps upload and a signal stronger than -70 dBm. If it’s weak, options include a mesh Wi-Fi node near the front of the house, or a doorbell model with a removable battery and local storage so it doesn’t depend on constant cloud connectivity.

Pro tip: Almost all video doorbells connect on 2.4 GHz only. If your router splits 2.4 and 5 GHz into separate networks, connect to the 2.4 GHz band during setup.

Step-by-Step Installation

Step 1: Kill the power

Flip the breaker that controls your doorbell circuit. Don’t guess — turn it off, then press your existing doorbell button. If it doesn’t ring, you’re good. If it does, you’ve got the wrong breaker.

Use a non-contact voltage tester on the doorbell wires before touching them. This takes 10 seconds and is non-negotiable.

Step 2: Remove the old doorbell

Most doorbells unscrew from the front or twist off a mounting bracket. Label the two wires if you can — though on a low-voltage AC circuit, polarity doesn’t matter for most models. Tuck the wires so they don’t fall back into the wall; a piece of tape or a clothespin works.

Step 3: Install the mounting bracket

Hold the new bracket against the wall and check that it covers any old screw holes or paint outlines. If your old doorbell was smaller, you may need to patch and paint, or choose a bracket with a larger footprint.

Feed the wires through the bracket’s center hole and screw the bracket into the wall. Use the included anchors if you’re not hitting a stud — doorbells get bumped and pried at, so secure mounting matters.

Step 4: Connect the wires

Loosen the terminal screws on the back of the doorbell, wrap each wire clockwise around a screw, and tighten firmly. Tug gently on each wire to confirm it’s secure. Loose connections are the number one cause of “my doorbell keeps losing power.”

If your model includes a power kit or chime connector, install it inside your indoor chime now, following the manufacturer’s diagram. This is usually two wires and a small module that clips or screws into place.

Step 5: Mount and power up

Snap or screw the doorbell onto the bracket. Restore the breaker. The doorbell should boot up — most play a chime or flash an LED within 30 seconds.

Step 6: Set up the app

Download the manufacturer’s app, create an account, and follow the pairing steps. You’ll connect to the doorbell’s temporary Wi-Fi hotspot, then enter your home network credentials.

During setup you’ll configure:

  • Motion zones (mask out the street or sidewalk to cut false alerts)
  • Notification sensitivity
  • Night vision and HDR settings
  • Chime behavior — mechanical, digital, or a plug-in wireless chime

Renters and No-Wire Situations

If you rent, or your door has no existing wiring, battery-powered doorbells solve both problems. Models from Ring, Eufy, and Arlo run for three to six months per charge and mount with adhesive plates or removable brackets.

Two caveats: battery models usually don’t trigger your existing indoor chime (you’ll use a plug-in chime instead), and they often lack the always-on recording that wired units provide. For renters, that’s usually a fair trade.

Troubleshooting the Most Common Problems

Doorbell reboots constantly: Almost always insufficient transformer power. Upgrade to 16V/30VA.

Indoor chime buzzes or hums: You skipped the power kit. Install it.

Motion alerts every two minutes: Your motion zone includes a busy street or swaying tree. Redraw the zone and lower sensitivity.

Doorbell won’t connect to Wi-Fi: Switch your phone to the 2.4 GHz band, move closer to the router during setup, and disable any VPN.

Video is choppy: Check upload speed at the door. If it’s under 2 Mbps, add a mesh node or switch to a model with local storage.

Final Thoughts

The whole job — from flipping the breaker to watching your first live feed — takes about 90 minutes for a wired install and 20 minutes for battery-powered. The prep work matters more than the installation itself: verify your transformer, know your chime type, and test your Wi-Fi before you buy.

Do those three checks and you’ll join the ranks of people who installed their own doorbell and spent the savings on something better than an electrician’s invoice.

item.title: Smart Lighting Setup Guide: Build Your System Right
item.description: A practical smart lighting setup guide covering hubs vs. Wi-Fi, bulb types, switch wiring, scenes, and automations that actually work.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The first smart bulb I ever installed was a disaster. It worked perfectly from my phone, which was exactly the problem — everyone else in the house kept flipping the wall switch off, which cut power to the bulb and made it unreachable until someone flipped it back on. Three weeks later I’d spent $60 on a “smart” light that behaved worse than a regular one.

That mistake taught me the single most important lesson in smart lighting: the technology is easy, but the design is hard. Anyone can screw in a bulb and download an app. Building a system that your family actually uses without complaints takes a bit of planning.

This guide walks you through that planning — the decisions that matter, the ones that don’t, and the setup order that saves you from redoing everything twice.

Step 1: Decide How Your Lights Will Be Controlled

Before you buy a single bulb, answer one question: do you want to control the bulbs, or the switch?

Option A: Smart bulbs

The bulb itself contains the radio and the logic. You control color, brightness, and scheduling per bulb. The catch: the light only works if the wall switch stays on.

Smart bulbs make sense for:

  • Lamps and floor lights that plug into outlets
  • Rooms where you want color or tunable white
  • Renters who can’t rewire anything

Option B: Smart switches

You replace the wall switch with a smart one, and use ordinary bulbs. The light responds to both the app and the physical switch, which is what most households actually want.

Smart switches make sense for:

  • Ceiling lights and recessed fixtures
  • Hallways, bathrooms, kitchens — anywhere people flip switches on autopilot
  • Multi-bulb fixtures where buying six smart bulbs is wasteful

Option C: Hybrid

Smart switches for the ceiling, smart bulbs in lamps. This is what most experienced smart-home people end up with, and it’s usually the right answer.

Practical tip: Walk through your home and count the fixtures you want to automate. If a fixture has more than two bulbs, a switch is almost always cheaper and simpler.

Step 2: Pick Your Protocol (This Is the Decision You’ll Regret Getting Wrong)

“Protocol” just means how your lights talk to each other. There are four realistic options.

Wi-Fi

The bulb connects directly to your router. No hub needed. Simple, but every device eats router capacity, and cheap Wi-Fi bulbs are notorious for dropping off the network. Fine for a handful of lights, painful at scale.

Zigbee and Z-Wave

Low-power mesh protocols. Each device relays signal for the others, so coverage gets better as you add lights. They require a hub (a small box that plugs into your router), but they’re fast, reliable, and don’t clog your Wi-Fi.

Thread / Matter

The newer standard. Thread is the mesh network; Matter is the common language that lets devices from different brands work together. If you’re starting fresh today and want your setup to still make sense in five years, this is the direction to lean.

Bluetooth

Fine for a single lamp in a dorm room. Not a real system. Skip it for anything permanent.

Rule of thumb: Under 10 lights and one room? Wi-Fi is fine. Whole house? Get a hub.

Step 3: Build in the Right Order

Most people buy bulbs first and figure out control later. Do it backwards.

  1. Pick your ecosystem. Choose one primary app or platform — Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, or a hub like SmartThings or Home Assistant. You can mix brands, but you want one place to manage everything.
  2. Start with one room. Not the whole house. Pick the room you use most and automate it completely. You’ll learn your preferences before spending real money.
  3. Buy switches for overheads, bulbs for lamps. As covered above.
  4. Add a hub if you’re going beyond a few devices. Zigbee/Thread hubs are cheap and solve most reliability complaints.
  5. Expand only after the first room runs smoothly for a month.

Step 4: Set Up Scenes, Not Just Individual Lights

The magic of smart lighting isn’t controlling one bulb from your phone. It’s controlling groups with one command.

A scene is a preset combination — specific lights at specific brightness and color. Examples that work well:

  • “Morning” — kitchen and bathroom at 100% cool white, hallway at 40%
  • “Movie” — living room overheads off, two lamps at 15% warm, hallway dim
  • “Goodnight” — everything off except a 5% path from living room to bedroom, auto-off in 10 minutes

Set these up in your app, then trigger them by voice, by a physical button, or automatically.

The best investment nobody talks about: a physical smart button or remote. Voice control is great until you’re hoarse or the kids are asleep. A $20 button stuck to the wall next to the light switch solves 80% of family complaints.

Step 5: Automations That Don’t Annoy You

Automations are rules: “when X happens, do Y.” The temptation is to automate everything. Don’t. Bad automations are worse than no automations.

These are the ones that consistently earn their keep:

  • Sunset trigger — exterior and living room lights come on at sunset, not a fixed time. Handles seasonal shifts automatically.
  • Motion in hallways and closets — 2-minute timeout, low brightness at night. Genuinely life-improving.
  • Away mode — random light patterns when you’re traveling.
  • Bedtime wind-down — lights shift warmer and dimmer starting 90 minutes before bed.

Skip these unless you have a specific reason:

  • Lights that turn on when you arrive home (they’ll blind you at the door)
  • Automations that override a switch someone just pressed manually
  • Anything that requires an internet connection to turn on a light

One more thing: set your lights to not respond to motion when you’ve manually turned them off. Most apps call this a “manual override” or “hold” setting. Without it, your bathroom light will turn back on two minutes after you deliberately turned it off, and you will hate your house.

Step 6: Handle the Family Problem

Smart lighting fails at the human layer more often than the technical one. Three fixes that work:

  1. Never remove a light switch. If a switch exists, it must still turn the light on and off. Smart switches do this natively. For smart bulbs, use a switch cover or a smart button mounted over the old switch.
  2. Label things clearly. “Kitchen Ceiling” not “Light 3.”
  3. Give everyone access. A shared household in the app takes two minutes and prevents the “why can’t I turn on my own light” conversation forever.

What to Buy First

If you want a concrete starting point:

  • One room, four lights: two smart switches for overheads, two smart bulbs for lamps, one hub, one button. Roughly $150–200.
  • Apartment, no wiring: smart plugs for lamps, smart bulbs for the two fixtures you use most, one button by the door. Roughly $80–120.

Buy one brand for your first room so setup stays sane. Once you understand the system, mixing brands gets much easier — especially if you stick to Matter-certified gear.

The Bottom Line

Smart lighting isn’t about having the most gadgets. It’s about walking into a room and having the light do what you want without thinking about it. Get the control method right, pick a protocol you won’t outgrow, start with one room, and always keep a physical switch working.

Do that, and you’ll end up with a system your household actually uses — instead of a $60 bulb nobody can turn on.

item.title: Home Network Security Tips That Actually Work
item.description: Practical home network security tips to protect your Wi-Fi, router, and smart devices from hackers, with step-by-step changes you can make today.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

A few years ago, a friend texted me in a mild panic. Her smart thermostat had started changing temperatures on its own, and her streaming accounts were logging out every day. She assumed it was a software glitch. It wasn’t. Someone had gotten onto her home network through an old router she’d never changed the password on, and they were poking around her connected devices for fun.

That story isn’t rare. Most home networks are protected by nothing more than a default router password and a Wi-Fi key that hasn’t changed since 2019. The good news is that securing your home network doesn’t require a degree in cybersecurity. It requires about an hour of focused effort and a handful of settings most people never touch.

Here’s what actually matters, in the order I’d do it.

Start With the Router, Because Everything Flows Through It

Your router is the front door to every device in your house. If someone gets in there, they can see your traffic, redirect you to fake websites, or use your connection for their own purposes. Most routers ship with weak defaults, so this is where you begin.

Change the admin password immediately

The default admin credentials for most routers are printed on a sticker or listed in the manual, which means they’re also published online. Log into your router’s settings page (usually something like 192.168.1.1), find the admin password field, and set something long and unique. Use a passphrase of four or five random words rather than a jumble of characters you’ll forget.

Update the firmware

Router manufacturers push security patches through firmware updates, and plenty of people never install them. Check your router’s settings for a firmware update option, or look up your exact model on the manufacturer’s site. Some newer routers update automatically — turn that on if it’s available.

Turn off WPS

Wi-Fi Protected Setup lets you connect devices by pressing a button or entering a short PIN. It’s convenient and it’s also a known weak point, because the PIN can be brute-forced. Disable it in your router settings. You’ll type your Wi-Fi password a few extra times and be safer for it.

Lock Down Your Wi-Fi Properly

Your wireless network is broadcasting to everyone within range, including anyone parked outside your house. A few settings make a big difference.

Use WPA3, or WPA2 if you must

In your router’s wireless security settings, choose WPA3 if your router supports it. If not, WPA2-AES is the next best option. Avoid WEP and WPA-TKIP entirely — both have been broken for years and offer almost no real protection.

Give your guest network a real job

Most routers let you run a separate guest network. Use it for visitors, and also for smart home gadgets like plugs, cameras, and TVs. These devices often have weak security and rarely get updates, so keeping them off your main network limits the damage if one gets compromised. Your laptops and phones stay on the primary network.

Hide nothing, but name wisely

Hiding your network name (SSID) doesn’t add meaningful security — anyone with basic tools can still find it. What does help is choosing a network name that doesn’t reveal your router model or your address. “SmithFamily_Netgear_5G” tells an attacker exactly what hardware to target.

Pay Attention to the Devices You Invite In

Every connected device is a potential entry point, and the average home now has more of them than people.

  • Change default passwords on cameras and smart plugs. A shocking number of these devices ship with “admin/admin” and stay that way. Check each one’s app or web interface and set a unique password.
  • Remove devices you no longer use. That old tablet in a drawer that’s still connected? It’s probably not getting security updates anymore. Disconnect it from your network.
  • Be careful with cheap unknown-brand gadgets. Some budget smart devices have been caught sending data to unexpected servers. If a $12 camera has no brand reputation, think twice before putting it inside your home.

Keep Your Own Devices Current

This part is less about the network and more about what’s on it, but it matters just as much.

Enable automatic updates on your phones, computers, and tablets. Install updates for your browser and its extensions — outdated browser plugins have been a common attack path for years. If you use a password manager, let it generate unique passwords for every account, because a breach on one site shouldn’t hand over the keys to everything else.

Two-factor authentication is worth turning on for your email especially. Your email is the reset point for almost every other account you own.

A Few Habits That Close the Gaps

Check who’s on your network. Most routers list connected devices in their settings or app. If you see something you don’t recognize, investigate it. Give your devices clear names so unfamiliar ones stand out.

Don’t do sensitive tasks on public Wi-Fi without protection. Coffee shop and airport networks are convenient and often unencrypted. If you’re logging into banking or work accounts, use your phone’s hotspot or a reputable VPN.

Reboot your router occasionally. It clears out temporary issues and forces it to reconnect cleanly. Once a month is plenty.

Write down what you changed. Keep a note of your router admin password and network credentials somewhere secure, ideally in a password manager. Future you will be grateful.

The Bottom Line

Home network security isn’t about buying expensive equipment or becoming a networking expert. It’s about closing the doors that ship open by default. Change the router password, update the firmware, use WPA3, separate your smart devices, and keep everything patched.

Do those five things this weekend and you’ll be safer than the vast majority of households on your street. My friend with the rogue thermostat? She did all of the above in one afternoon, and nothing strange has happened since.

item.title: Best Wi-Fi Router for Home: 2025 Buyer's Guide
item.description: Stop overpaying for internet you're not getting. Learn how to pick the best Wi-Fi router for your home, plus top picks for every budget and house size.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Your internet provider charges you for 500 Mbps. You run a speed test on your phone while standing next to the router and get 480. Walk into the bedroom and it drops to 40. Try to take a video call from the backyard and it falls apart entirely.

This is the most common complaint I hear from homeowners, and nine times out of ten, the ISP isn’t the problem. The router is. Most people are still using the box their provider handed them three years ago — a device that was cheap when it was new and is now a bottleneck for every phone, laptop, TV, and smart bulb in the house.

Here’s the good news: a router upgrade is one of the highest-return purchases you can make for your home. A $150 router can transform a frustrating network into one that just works. But only if you buy the right one. The wrong router — even an expensive one — can leave you with the same dead zones and dropped calls.

This guide walks you through how to choose, what actually matters (and what’s marketing noise), and the specific routers worth your money in 2025.

First, Answer Three Questions

Before you look at a single product, get clear on your situation. Router shopping without this step is how people end up with a $400 device that doesn’t solve their problem.

1. How big is your home?

  • Under 1,500 sq ft: a single good router usually covers it.
  • 1,500–3,000 sq ft: a single high-end router or a two-piece mesh system.
  • Over 3,000 sq ft, or multiple floors with thick walls: mesh is almost always the answer.

2. How many devices are connected? Count them. Phones, laptops, tablets, smart TVs, streaming sticks, game consoles, thermostats, doorbells, security cameras, robot vacuums. A typical family home now runs 20–40 devices. Older routers choke on that.

3. What do you actually do online?

  • Browsing, email, streaming one 4K show: any modern router handles this.
  • Multiple 4K streams at once, video calls, gaming: you need Wi-Fi 6 and decent processing power.
  • Work-from-home with large file transfers, or heavy gaming: Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7, and prioritize low latency.

The Specs That Actually Matter

Wi-Fi 6 vs. Wi-Fi 6E vs. Wi-Fi 7

Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) is the current baseline. If you’re buying a router today and it doesn’t support Wi-Fi 6, skip it.

Wi-Fi 6E adds a new 6 GHz band. Think of it as a private highway with almost no traffic. It’s faster and less congested, but only devices that support 6E can use it — which right now means newer phones, laptops, and TVs. It’s a nice future-proofing feature, not a must-have.

Wi-Fi 7 is the newest standard. It’s genuinely faster and handles many devices better, but you’ll pay a premium, and most homes won’t notice the difference yet. Buy it if you’re a tech enthusiast or plan to keep the router for five-plus years. Otherwise, Wi-Fi 6 or 6E is the sweet spot.

Bands: Dual vs. Tri-Band

A dual-band router has 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. Tri-band adds a second 5 GHz (or 6 GHz) band. More bands mean more capacity for multiple devices. In a busy home, tri-band makes a real difference.

MU-MIMO and OFDMA

These let the router talk to multiple devices at once instead of one at a time. Almost every Wi-Fi 6 router has them. Don’t pay extra for them — just confirm they’re there.

Ethernet Ports

Count them. You want at least four LAN ports if you have wired devices like a desktop, console, or NAS. Some budget routers only have two.

What You Can Ignore

  • “Gaming” branding: Often just a repackaged router with a QoS toggle and RGB lights.
  • Antenna count: Six antennas don’t automatically beat four. Design matters more.
  • Theoretical top speeds (like “AXE11000”): These are marketing numbers. Real-world speeds are far lower.

Single Router vs. Mesh: The Real Decision

This is the choice that trips up most buyers.

A single router is simpler and cheaper. It works great in smaller homes or apartments where the router can sit centrally.

A mesh system uses two or three units placed around the house. They hand off devices seamlessly as you move room to room. If you have dead zones, mesh is the fix — not a bigger, more expensive single router. No single router, no matter how powerful, reliably covers 3,000 sq ft through drywall and brick.

Actionable tip: Before buying mesh, try moving your current router. Central location, off the floor, away from metal, microwaves, and fish tanks. I’ve seen people solve “dead zone” problems entirely by moving the router from a closet to a hallway shelf.

Top Picks by Situation

Best Overall for Most Homes: TP-Link Archer AX55

Around $100, this is the router I recommend most often. Wi-Fi 6, solid range for apartments and smaller houses, four Ethernet ports, and reliable firmware. It won’t win benchmarks, but it does everything a normal household needs without fuss.

Best for Large Homes: TP-Link Deco X60 (3-pack)

A tri-band mesh system that covers up to 7,000 sq ft. Setup takes about 15 minutes through an app. It handles 30+ devices without breaking a sweat and eliminates dead zones on multiple floors. For the price, it’s the most practical mesh system for most families.

Best for Gamers and Power Users: ASUS RT-AX86U Pro

Low latency, excellent QoS controls, and a 2.5 Gbps port for fast fiber connections. If you game competitively or run a home office with heavy uploads, this is worth the extra cost.

Best Budget Pick: TP-Link Archer AX21

Under $80, Wi-Fi 6, and genuinely good for a one-bedroom apartment or a small home with modest needs. Don’t expect it to cover a two-story house, but for the price, it’s hard to beat.

Best Future-Proof: ASUS RT-BE96U (Wi-Fi 7)

Expensive, but if you want to buy once and forget it for five years, Wi-Fi 7 with a 6 GHz band is the way to go. Only worth it if you have multi-gig internet and newer devices.

Setup Tips That Double Your Performance

Buying the right router is half the battle. Placement is the other half.

  1. Put it central and high. The router broadcasts outward and down. A central hallway shelf beats a corner office every time.
  2. Avoid the kitchen and utility rooms. Microwaves, refrigerators, and metal appliances interfere with signal.
  3. Update the firmware immediately. Out-of-the-box firmware is often months old and may have security gaps.
  4. Change the default admin password. Do this before anything else.
  5. Separate your bands if you have older devices. Some smart home gadgets struggle with combined SSIDs.
  6. Use the 5 GHz band for anything that stays put — TVs, consoles, desktops. Save 2.4 GHz for devices that need range.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to buy my own router, or is the ISP’s fine? If you’re paying a monthly rental fee (often $10–$15), you’re spending $120–$180 a year on a device you don’t own. Buying your own usually pays for itself in under a year and performs better.

Will a better router give me faster internet? Only up to the speed you’re paying for. If your plan is 100 Mbps, a $300 router won’t make it faster. But it will make that 100 Mbps actually reach every room.

How long should a router last? Five to seven years is reasonable. Replace it sooner if it’s overheating, dropping connections, or can’t handle your device count.

Is Wi-Fi 7 worth it right now? For most people, no. Wi-Fi 6E is the better value in 2025. Wi-Fi 7 makes sense if you’re buying for the long haul and have the devices and internet plan to match.

The Bottom Line

The best Wi-Fi router for your home isn’t the most expensive one — it’s the one that matches your square footage, device count, and internet speed. For most households, a solid Wi-Fi 6 router under $150 or a tri-band mesh system will solve every problem you’re currently blaming on your ISP.

Start by measuring your home and counting your devices. Then buy for that reality, not for the spec sheet. And whatever you choose, spend ten minutes on placement and setup. It’s the cheapest performance upgrade you’ll ever get.

item.title: How to Speed Up Home Internet: 12 Fixes That Work
item.description: Slow Wi-Fi? Learn how to speed up home internet with 12 practical fixes—from router placement to DNS tweaks—no technician visit required.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last Tuesday, my neighbor Dana called me in a panic. Her internet had crawled to a halt mid-Zoom call, and her provider’s only advice was to “restart the router.” She’d already done that three times. Twenty minutes later, we found the real culprit: her router was sitting inside a metal media cabinet, behind a flat-screen TV, broadcasting through two walls to reach her home office. We moved it four feet. Her speed test jumped from 12 Mbps to 210 Mbps.

Most slow internet isn’t a provider problem. It’s a physics and configuration problem. And the good news is that you can fix almost all of it yourself in an afternoon. Here’s exactly how.

First, Run a Proper Speed Test

Before changing anything, you need a baseline. But not all speed tests are equal.

  • Test on a wired connection if possible. Plug a laptop directly into your router with an Ethernet cable. This tells you what speed you’re actually paying for and removes Wi-Fi from the equation.
  • Test at different times of day. If your speed tanks every evening around 8 PM, that’s congestion on your provider’s network, not your equipment. No router tweak will fix that.
  • Use the same server each time. Speedtest.net, Fast.com, and Google’s built-in test can give wildly different numbers. Pick one and stick with it.

Write down three numbers: wired speed, Wi-Fi speed next to the router, and Wi-Fi speed in the room where you actually use the internet. Those three numbers tell you where the problem lives.

Fix Your Router Placement (This Is Usually the Whole Problem)

Wi-Fi is radio. It behaves like radio. That means:

  • Walls eat signal. Drywall costs you a little. Brick, concrete, and plaster with metal lath cost you a lot. Every wall between you and the router cuts throughput.
  • Metal reflects and blocks. Filing cabinets, mirrors, fish tanks, metal shelving, and yes, that stylish media console—all of them wreck your signal.
  • Height matters. Routers radiate outward and slightly down. A shelf four to six feet off the floor beats the floor itself every time.
  • Central location wins. A router in the corner of the house means half its signal goes into the yard.

Action step: Put your router in the most central, open, elevated spot you can manage. Not in a closet. Not behind the TV. Not on the floor next to the subwoofer.

Switch to the Right Wi-Fi Band

If your router broadcasts both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz networks, you’ve probably been connecting to the wrong one.

  • 2.4 GHz travels farther and through walls better, but it’s slower and crowded—microwaves, baby monitors, garage door openers, and every neighbor’s router share that band.
  • 5 GHz is much faster but has shorter range.

The fix: Connect devices that stay in one place—smart TVs, gaming consoles, desktop PCs—to the 5 GHz network. Use 2.4 GHz for things far from the router or that don’t need much bandwidth, like smart plugs and sensors.

If your router combines both bands into one network name and you’re getting inconsistent speeds, log into the router settings and split them into separate names. It’s a five-minute change that solves a lot of mystery slowdowns.

Change Your Wi-Fi Channel

In apartment buildings and dense neighborhoods, everyone’s router is shouting on the same channel. It’s like a crowded room where nobody can hear each other.

For 2.4 GHz: Only channels 1, 6, and 11 don’t overlap. Use a free app like WiFiman or NetSpot to see which of those three is least crowded, then set your router to that channel manually. Auto mode often picks poorly.

For 5 GHz: There are far more channels available, so congestion is less of an issue—but if you’re in a dense building, it’s still worth scanning and picking a clear one.

Update Router Firmware and Replace Ancient Hardware

Router manufacturers push firmware updates that fix bugs, patch security holes, and occasionally improve performance. Most people never install them.

Log into your router’s admin page (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1) and check for a firmware update option. Some newer routers update automatically through their companion app—check that it’s enabled.

Now the harder truth: if your router is more than five years old, it’s probably your bottleneck. Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) routers handle multiple devices dramatically better than older standards, and Wi-Fi 6E adds a whole new 6 GHz band that’s basically empty. If you’re paying for 500 Mbps and your router tops out at 100, you’re lighting money on fire every month.

Also check your modem. If your provider gave you a combo modem/router unit from 2016, ask if you can use your own equipment. Most ISPs allow it, and a $150 router will often outperform their rental.

Use Ethernet for Anything That Doesn’t Move

Every device you move off Wi-Fi frees up bandwidth and airtime for everything else.

  • Gaming consoles: Ethernet. Always.
  • Desktop computers: Ethernet if the run is reasonable.
  • Smart TVs and streaming boxes: Ethernet if you can, especially for 4K.
  • Work-from-home setups: Ethernet for video calls if at all possible.

If running cable is impractical, powerline adapters or MoCA adapters (which use your existing coax wiring) are solid alternatives. They beat Wi-Fi through thick walls in most cases.

Trim the Device Herd

Open your router’s admin page and look at the connected devices list. You will almost certainly find things you forgot existed.

  • An old tablet still pulling updates
  • A smart TV in the guest room that’s been streaming something for three days
  • A neighbor who guessed your password in 2019

Kick off anything you don’t recognize, change your Wi-Fi password, and use WPA3 or WPA2 security. Then go through your smart home devices and ask honestly: does the fish tank light really need Wi-Fi?

Try a Better DNS Server

DNS doesn’t affect raw download speed, but it affects how fast websites feel. Every time you type a URL, your device asks a DNS server to translate it into an IP address. If your ISP’s DNS server is slow, every page load starts with a delay.

Switch to Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8). You can set this on your router so every device benefits, or per-device if you prefer. Many people report noticeably snappier browsing after this change alone.

Consider a Mesh System for Large Homes

If you live in a house over about 2,000 square feet, or a home with tricky layouts, a single router will struggle no matter where you put it. A mesh Wi-Fi system uses multiple units that hand off devices seamlessly as you move around.

Two important notes:

  1. Mesh nodes need to be placed where they still get a strong signal from the main unit. Putting a node in the dead zone doesn’t fix the dead zone.
  2. Mesh beats a cheap range extender almost every time. Extenders halve your bandwidth and create a second network name; mesh doesn’t.

Know When It’s Actually Your Provider

Sometimes it really is them. Call your ISP if:

  • Your wired speed is consistently well below what you pay for
  • Speeds crater at the same time every day (network congestion)
  • You’re seeing high latency and packet loss, not just low speed
  • Your modem shows frequent disconnects in its event log

Before you call, document your speed tests with timestamps. It makes the conversation much shorter.

The 30-Minute Action Plan

If you only do five things, do these:

  1. Move the router to a central, open, elevated spot
  2. Connect stationary devices via Ethernet
  3. Split your 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz networks and assign devices correctly
  4. Update firmware and change your Wi-Fi channel
  5. Switch your DNS to 1.1.1.1

Most people see a meaningful improvement from steps one through three alone. And if you’re still stuck on a router from the Obama administration, treat yourself. Your internet has been waiting for an upgrade.

item.title: Home Entertainment System Setup: A Practical Guide
item.description: Build a home entertainment system that actually works. Learn how to choose a TV, match a soundbar, hide cables, and calibrate your setup step by step.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Most people set up a new TV the same way: unbox it, plug in the power, mount it on the wall, and call it done. Three months later they’re still using the built-in speakers, the picture looks washed out, and there’s a nest of cables behind the console that nobody wants to touch.

A properly built home entertainment system isn’t about spending more money. It’s about making a few deliberate decisions in the right order. Get the foundation right and everything else falls into place — the picture, the sound, and the way the whole thing feels in the room.

Here’s how to do it without wasting a weekend or buying gear you don’t need.

Start With the Room, Not the Gear

Before you look at a single product page, measure your space. The room dictates almost every choice you’ll make afterward.

Seating distance matters more than screen size. A common rule of thumb for 4K TVs is to sit at a distance of roughly 1 to 1.5 times the screen’s vertical height. For a 65-inch TV, that’s about 6.5 to 10 feet. Sit too close and you’ll see pixel structure and scan lines during fast motion. Sit too far and you lose the benefit of 4K entirely.

Check your wall for studs. If you’re wall-mounting, you need at least two studs behind the bracket, or a mounting solution rated for drywall alone. A stud finder costs $20 and saves you from a very expensive mistake.

Watch for window glare. A TV placed directly opposite a south-facing window will look terrible during the day no matter how bright it is. If you can’t move the TV, plan for blackout curtains or a matte-finish screen.

Count your outlets before you buy anything. One outlet behind the TV is rarely enough. You’ll likely need power for the TV, a streaming device, a soundbar, and possibly a game console. A single surge protector with a long cord solves most of this.

Choosing the Right TV for Your Space

Not every room needs an OLED. Here’s a quick way to decide.

Bright rooms with lots of daytime light do better with a QLED or mini-LED panel. They push higher brightness and resist glare better than OLED.

Dark rooms and dedicated movie spaces are where OLED shines. Perfect blacks and wide viewing angles make a real difference when you’re watching in low light.

Gaming setups need to check three boxes: HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, and low input lag. Most mid-range TVs from the last two years include these, but verify before buying.

One thing people overlook: the TV’s smart interface. If you’re going to use the built-in apps, make sure the OS is one you can live with. Otherwise, plan on a separate streaming device from day one.

Sound: Where Most Setups Fall Short

A $1,200 TV with built-in speakers sounds worse than a $300 soundbar. This is the single biggest upgrade most people can make.

For small rooms (under 200 sq ft): A 2.0 or 2.1 soundbar is plenty. Look for one with a dedicated center channel — it makes dialogue much clearer.

For medium rooms: Step up to a 3.1 system with a subwoofer. The center channel handles dialogue, the sub handles low-end, and the left/right channels handle everything else.

For dedicated theaters: A 5.1.2 or 7.1.2 setup with upward-firing or in-ceiling speakers gives you true Dolby Atmos. This is where the investment starts to matter.

Placement tip: Put the soundbar at ear level, not on the floor. If it’s below the TV, angle it slightly upward. Subwoofers work best in a corner or against a wall — bass waves build up there.

If you’re running a receiver-based system, calibrate it with the included microphone. It takes 10 minutes and corrects for room acoustics in ways manual settings can’t.

Cables, Power, and Hiding the Mess

This is the part everyone dreads, but it’s also the part that makes the biggest visual difference.

Run cables before you mount anything. Once the TV is on the wall, threading cables becomes a two-person job with a lot of swearing.

Use in-wall rated cables if you’re running anything through drywall. Standard HDMI cables aren’t rated for in-wall use and can fail or create a fire hazard.

Consider a cable management box for the console area. A single box hides the power strip, router, and excess cable slack. It costs $25 and transforms the look of the space.

Label both ends of every cable. You’ll thank yourself in two years when you’re swapping a device.

For wall-mounted TVs, a recessed media box behind the TV keeps everything flush. If you’re not cutting into drywall, a paintable cable channel is the next best option.

Calibrating the Picture (Free and Worth It)

Out of the box, most TVs are set to “Vivid” or “Dynamic” mode, which oversaturates colors and crushes detail. Switch to “Movie” or “Cinema” mode immediately.

Then adjust these three settings:

  1. Backlight: Set based on room brightness, not maxed out. Around 40-60% for evening viewing.
  2. Contrast: Start at 80% and adjust until whites are bright but not blown out.
  3. Sharpness: Turn it down to zero or near zero. TV sharpness settings add artificial edge enhancement that makes content look worse, not better.

For a more precise calibration, use a free test pattern video on YouTube. It takes 15 minutes and gets you 90% of the way to a professional calibration.

Connecting Everything Without Headaches

Use the right HDMI ports. Most TVs have one or two “enhanced” ports that support 4K at 120Hz. Your game console and primary streaming device should go there.

Enable HDMI-CEC. This lets your TV remote turn on the soundbar and switch inputs automatically. It’s called different things on different brands — Anynet+, Bravia Sync, Simplink — but it all does the same thing.

Connect streaming devices directly to the TV, not the receiver, if you want the best picture quality. Receivers sometimes strip HDR metadata.

For older receivers without eARC, run audio through optical. You lose lossless formats, but it works reliably.

A Realistic Budget Breakdown

Here’s what a solid mid-range setup looks like:

  • TV (55-65"): $600-1,000
  • Soundbar with subwoofer: $300-500
  • Streaming device: $50-100
  • HDMI cables and mounts: $60-100
  • Cable management: $30-50

Total: roughly $1,000-1,750. You can absolutely spend less, but this range gets you a system that looks and sounds genuinely good.

The Bottom Line

A great home entertainment setup isn’t about buying the most expensive gear. It’s about matching components to your room, getting the sound right, and taking 30 minutes to hide the cables and calibrate the picture.

Start with the room. Pick a TV that fits your lighting. Don’t skip the soundbar. Hide the mess. Then calibrate.

Do those five things and your setup will outperform systems that cost twice as much.

item.title: Home Network Security: 12 Best Practices That Work
item.description: Protect your home Wi-Fi from hackers with these practical network security tips—from router settings to guest networks and firmware updates.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

A few years ago, a family in my neighborhood noticed their smart TV buffering constantly. Odd, but not alarming—until the internet provider called. Someone had been using their network to run a small file-sharing operation, and it had been going on for months. The router password? Still the default one printed on the sticker.

That story isn’t unusual. Your home network is the front door to every device you own: laptops with tax documents, phones with banking apps, cameras pointed at your living room. Most people lock that door with a password they’ve never changed. Here’s how to actually secure it, without needing a degree in computer science.

Start With the Router (It’s the Weakest Link)

Change the Default Admin Credentials

Every router ships with a username and password like “admin/admin.” These are publicly documented. If you’ve never logged into your router, do it today—usually by typing 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 into a browser. Change both the admin username and password to something unique.

Update Firmware Regularly

Router manufacturers patch security holes through firmware updates, but they can’t force you to install them. Log into your router’s admin panel and check for updates every few months. Some newer routers have an auto-update option—turn it on. If your router hasn’t received a firmware update in over two years, it’s probably time for a new one.

Disable WPS

Wi-Fi Protected Setup lets you connect devices by pressing a button, which sounds convenient until you learn that its PIN method can be brute-forced in hours. Turn WPS off in your router settings. Connecting a new device manually takes thirty extra seconds.

Lock Down Your Wi-Fi

Use WPA3 (or WPA2 if You Must)

Check your wireless security setting. If it says WEP or “open,” you’re essentially broadcasting your traffic to the street. WPA3 is the current standard; WPA2-AES is acceptable if your devices don’t support WPA3. Anything older should be replaced.

Make Your Password Long, Not Clever

“Fluffy2019!” is not a strong password—it’s a guessable one. Aim for at least 16 characters, mixing words in a way that’s memorable to you but not obvious: something like “purplecouch7lampmonday.” Length beats complexity every time. And never reuse your Wi-Fi password for other accounts.

Hide Your Network Name? Skip It

Hiding your SSID (network name) sounds stealthy, but it doesn’t stop determined attackers and it breaks your own devices’ ability to reconnect smoothly. A strong password does far more for you.

Segment Your Network

Set Up a Guest Network

Your guest Wi-Fi isn’t just for visitors. Put smart bulbs, TVs, and other IoT gadgets on it. These devices often have weak security and rarely get updates. Keeping them on a separate network means a compromised smart plug can’t reach your laptop.

Consider a VLAN If You’re Technical

More advanced routers let you create VLANs—virtual networks that isolate device groups. It’s overkill for most homes, but if you work from home with sensitive data, it’s worth exploring.

Pay Attention to the Devices Themselves

Change Default Passwords on Everything

That IP camera with the password “12345”? It’s a known entry point. Every connected device—cameras, printers, smart speakers—should have its default login changed the day you set it up.

Enable Automatic Updates

Phones, computers, and even smart TVs push security patches. Turning on automatic updates means you don’t have to think about it. For devices that don’t support auto-updates, set a calendar reminder to check quarterly.

Turn Off Features You Don’t Use

Remote access, UPnP, and file sharing are convenient until they’re not. If you don’t use your router’s remote management feature, disable it. UPnP, in particular, lets apps open ports without asking—a favorite trick of malware.

Monitor and Maintain

Check Who’s on Your Network

Most routers list connected devices in the admin panel. Scan it occasionally. If you see a device you don’t recognize, investigate immediately and change your Wi-Fi password. Some routers and apps (like Fing) will alert you to new devices automatically.

Watch for Warning Signs

Sluggish internet, unexpected reboots, or a router admin page that won’t load properly can all signal trouble. Don’t dismiss them.

Back Up Your Router Configuration
